$comment: The DNS records this zone is supposed to have, as a plan `tools/zone-setup.mjs records`
applies and re-applies. It is declarative and idempotent: running it twice changes
nothing the second time, and running it after someone edits the dashboard puts the zone
back. `records` without --apply prints the diff and changes nothing.
Measured on 2026-08-09, before the nameserver move: ordoia.com resolved to
162.255.119.119 (Namecheap's parking page), with MX at eforward1-5.registrar-servers.com
and Namecheap's SPF include. Cloudflare's zone scan imports whatever it finds, so all of
that arrives in the new zone unless it is removed deliberately.
Removing the apex address record before the nameservers move is what makes the ordering
in DEPLOY.md safe rather than a race: with no proxied web record at the apex, the zone
can go active without Cloudflare serving a single byte, so the hardening does not have
to win a race against the first request.
$removeComment: Matched on type and name, and on content when `contentMatches` is given (a regular
expression). No content matcher on the address records is deliberate: the invariant is
'no A or AAAA at the apex', which is the same sentence `evaluateZone` asserts, so it is
stated once and a rotated parking IP cannot slip past it.
Namecheap's free Email Forwarding is only available on their own nameservers, so these
MX records stop working at the cutover whatever we do. They are removed rather than
left, because an MX record pointing at a service that no longer accepts your mail is
worse than none: it accepts the message and drops it.
$ensureComment: Namecheap Private Email, taken from its panel on 2026-08-09 rather than from memory.
Mail is deliberately configured BEFORE the nameservers move, not after: the registrar's
own forwarding stops working at the cutover, and an MX record pointing at a service that
no longer accepts your mail is worse than no MX record, because it accepts the message
and drops it.
Exactly one SPF record may exist for a domain. The registrar's is in `remove` above and
this one replaces it; two would make both fail rather than merge.
The DKIM value is a public key. It is public by definition — it is published in DNS so
that anyone can verify a signature with it — so it belongs in this file. The private half
never leaves Namecheap. It is longer than the 255 bytes a single DNS character-string
holds; Cloudflare accepts the whole value and splits it on serve, which is why it is
written here as one string and verified afterwards with dig rather than pre-chunked.
DMARC at p=none first. A practice that publishes a posture should have a DMARC record,
and quarantine before a single message has been observed is how you lose your own mail.
Move to p=quarantine once the aggregate reports show the mailbox's own sends aligning.
The apex CNAME IS here, and the reason it is has to be written down, because the
documentation says the opposite. Cloudflare's custom-domain page states that once the
nameservers point at Cloudflare it 'will proceed by creating a CNAME record for you'.
That is true of the dashboard flow. It is not true of `POST /pages/projects/{p}/domains`:
measured 2026-08-09, the API accepted the domain, reported status 'pending', and sat
there with verification_data.error_message = 'CNAME record not set' while the zone had
no address record at all and ordoia.com did not resolve.
So the record is ours to create. The order still matters and is the documented one:
associate the domain with the Pages project FIRST, then add the CNAME. Cloudflare warns
that a CNAME added without the association resolves to a 522.
It must be proxied — orange-cloud. A DNS-only CNAME at the apex would bypass the zone
entirely, so none of the settings check 22 asserts would apply to the traffic, and the
certificate would not be Cloudflare's to issue.
